correctness.rationale: The proof uses only standard incidence identities for a closed \(\{k,3\}\) polyhedral surface. Face-edge counting gives \(E=4k\); trivalence gives \(V=8k/3\) and hence \(3\mid k\). Face-neighbourliness gives \(E\ge28\), so divisibility sharpens \(k\ge7\) to \(k\ge9\). Euler's formula yields \(g=2k/3-3\). Because every edge belongs to one unordered face pair, the repeated-adjacency surplus is exactly \(E-28=4k-28\). At \(k=9\) each face has nine incident boundary edges spread over seven other faces, forcing local excess degree \(2\). Under \(e_{ij}\le2\) those excesses are \(0\) or \(1\), hence the doubled-pair graph is simple \(2\)-regular; the only cycle partitions of eight with parts at least three are \(8\), \(5+3\), and \(4+4\). No experiment is used to prove a universal step.

value.rationale: The focal literature emphasizes that two new/known eight-faced polyhedra unexpectedly share the same face vector and the same \(20/8\) edge-multiplicity split despite being combinatorially inequivalent. The theorem explains that coincidence: those numerical data are forced at the smallest possible trivalent equivelar face-neighbourly level. It also reduces the doubled-adjacency combinatorics to exactly three natural cycle types and identifies \(5+3\) as the sole type not represented by the two compared examples. This gives a concrete structural target for future realization or obstruction work rather than a routine recount of either construction.
